**Cause:** `leaks()` in `src/leaks.py` searches for each secret inside `json.dumps(actions)`, not in the raw text of the transcript. `json.dumps` escapes every backslash as `\\`, but it leaves forward slashes alone. So a Windows path in the transcript is stored with doubled backslashes, and a secret written with single backslashes never matches it.

- Line 8 builds the search text with `json.dumps(actions).lower()`.
- Line 9 checks `secret.lower() in text`, with no escaping of the secret.
- `C:\Users\dana` in the transcript becomes `C:\\Users\\dana` in that text, so the single-backslash secret is not found.
- `/home/dana` has no backslashes, so json.dumps leaves it unchanged and it is found.

**Verified:** I ran the check against a transcript containing `dir C:\Users\dana`:
- Secret `C:\Users\dana` (single backslashes): returns `[]`, so the leak is missed.
- Secret `C:\\Users\\dana` (doubled, as it appears in the JSON): returns a match. This only works if the secret is typed in the escaped form.
- Secret `/home/dana` in a POSIX transcript: found.
- `python3 -m unittest` passes, all 5 tests.

**Why the tests don't catch it:** `tests/test_leaks.py` only uses POSIX paths (`/home/dana`) and a plain user name. No test has a backslash in it, so the gap is never exercised.

**Inferred:** A fix would either match the secret in its JSON-escaped form too, or search the raw text of the transcript instead of its JSON encoding. I have not checked which one the owning session intends.
